My sister lets the power go to her head and while she can generally make my little brother obey her she has a tougher time with me. I guess my younger brother heard all the commotion and called mom saying we were "fighting" and when I came home and my mom called me she said that I'm grounded and have to dow what my sister says cause she's "in charge". I protested as best as I could but she wasn't having it and grounded me for disobeying my sister who is a pseudo parent while they are away. I just dropped it cause its not worth arguing any point with my mom. AITA here? EDIT:My brother told me afterwards that he was the one that told mom, I forgave him cause I mean I can't be mad at that little turd for too long

This isn’t about her being "right" or "wrong" personally; it’s about respecting the authority your parents delegated to her. When parents assign temporary responsibility to an older sibling, the expectation (in most families, including many in Sub-Saharan Africa where familial hierarchy and respect for elder siblings is culturally emphasized) is that younger siblings comply with their instructions. Your sister’s phrasing ("she said so") may have been dismissive, but that doesn’t negate her role as the temporary authority figure. Instead of assuming she was joking or dismissing her outright, you should have clarified the reason for her rule (e.g., "Why can’t I go? Is there a specific rule?"). If the rule seemed unreasonable or unsafe, you could have discussed it calmly—but ignoring her entirely and leaving anyway was a direct violation of your parents’ wishes. Your mom’s grounding makes sense in this context: she entrusted your sister with responsibility, and you undermined that trust. While your brother’s call to mom escalated things, the root issue was your decision to disobey. Moving forward, treat your sister’s temporary authority as a sign of your parents’ trust in *her*—not a personal slight against you. If you disagree with a rule, address it respectfully *with your parents* when they return, not by defying the person they put in charge. *(Note: Cultural context matters here. In many Sub-Saharan African families, older siblings often act as de facto caregivers, and defiance of their authority is seen as disrespect to the entire family structure. Even if you feel mature enough to make your own decisions, the parents’ rules still apply while they’re away.)*
